summary: Reorganizes the names of already-allocated TLV types and type extensions in the MANET parameters registries from RFC 5444 so the names are used appropriately. It changes nothing in how protocols behave. It also updates the Expert Review guidelines so future names are chosen consistently.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tidies up the names in the registries of the mobile ad hoc network packet format. Nothing on the network changes. What changes is which name belongs to which number, so that new parts can be added to the format later without being given a misleading name.

how are manet tlv registries named
subtitle: A pure naming cleanup of the MANET TLV registries so type extensions can be allocated without misleading names.

tldr.problem: A MANET TLV is identified by a type and a type extension, and some TLV types were given a name that implied all 256 type extensions under them were versions of the same thing. That left the unused extensions either impossible to allocate or wrongly named when they were.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC changes the naming of already-allocated TLV types and type extensions in the three MANET Parameters subregistries, so a name now belongs to the exact full type it describes, and the parent type is left described only by its number.
tldr.outcome: Nothing about how any protocol behaves changes: the naming was already used in effect by RFC 6130 and RFC 7181. The RFC also updates the Expert Review guidelines so that future allocations are named consistently. RFC 7631 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5444 and was later updated by RFC 7722.

today: RFC 7631 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5444 and was itself updated by RFC 7722. It has not been obsoleted, and the registries it rewrote are the ones in use.

sections.title: A Naming Cleanup, Not a Protocol Change
sections.content:
This document reorganizes and rationalizes the naming of TLVs, meaning type-length-value structures, defined by RFC 5444 and recorded by IANA in three subregistries of the "Mobile Ad hoc NETwork (MANET) Parameters" registry: "Packet TLV Types", "Message TLV Types" and "Address Block TLV Types". The only changes are of naming. Nothing in the document changes the operation of any protocol.

The reason is that TLVs are allocated in two different ways, and only one of them suits a name. The first, less common, form is where the allocation of the TLV type has defined, but not necessarily allocated, all the type extensions for that TLV type. The Address Block TLV LINK_METRIC specified in RFC 7181 is an example: all of its type extensions are available for allocation for different definitions of link metric, so it is appropriate to apply the name LINK_METRIC to the type and to all the full types that correspond to it. Type extensions can then be named individually or simply referred to by their number.

The second, more common, form is where the allocation of the TLV type has defined only type extension 0, and possibly type extension 1. The Address Block TLV LINK_STATUS defined in RFC 6130 is an example, where only type extension 0 is allocated. It is not reasonable to assume that the remaining 255 type extensions will be allocated to forms of LINK_STATUS, and other forms of link status are already catered to by the registry for values of the LINK_STATUS TLV introduced in RFC 7188. The name LINK_STATUS should therefore be attached to the specific type extension, that is, to the full type, and not to the TLV type when used with any other type extensions. That was not done when the TLV type was first registered. The effect is that the type extensions 1 to 255 are left either unavailable for allocation, under a strict reading, or counterintuitively named for whatever function they end up serving.

The purpose of the document is to change how names of the second form are applied and recorded in the IANA registries, and to give guidelines for future allocations. LINK_STATUS becomes the name of the full type made up of TLV type 3 and TLV type extension 0, and ceases to be the name of TLV type 3. The type itself is left unnamed and specified only by number, because it is not clear what other TLVs might be defined for its other type extensions. The RFC notes that this naming is already used, in effect, in RFC 6130 and RFC 7181, the main users of allocated TLVs: RFC 6130 indicates that all usage of LINK_STATUS refers to that TLV with type extension 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Some TLV names were given to a whole family of numbers when only one of them was ever defined. That left the rest of the family unusable, or waiting to be named after whatever they ended up carrying. This document attaches each name to the exact number it describes, and leaves the family name free for whatever comes next.

sections.title: Types and Type Extensions
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC sets out the conventions. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. All references to elements such as "packet", "message" and "TLV" refer to those defined in RFC 5444.

The structural point is short. A TLV has a type, of one octet, and a type extension, of one octet, and the two together form a full type of two octets. A TLV may omit the type extension when it is zero, but that applies only to its representation on the wire: it still has a type extension of zero. A TLV type defines an IANA registry of type extensions for that type, so every type owns a list of extensions, and it is the extension that names the particular meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of information in a MANET packet is identified by two numbers, one for the kind and one for the version of that kind. Together they make a full type, and the version number is what this document is about.

sections.title: The Rules for Naming Future Allocations
sections.content:
Section 3.1 replaces the Expert Review evaluation guidelines of RFC 5444 for the "Packet TLV Types", "Message TLV Types" and "Address Block TLV Types" registries, adding to the guidelines already given in Section 6.1 of that RFC.

The first rule keeps the existing case. If the requested TLV type immediately defines, but not necessarily allocates, all the corresponding type extensions for versions of that type, then a common name SHOULD be assigned for the TLV type. This case is unchanged by the document, and currently covers the TLV types named ICV, TIMESTAMP and LINK_METRIC, as well as the HELLO Message-Type-specific TLVs defined in RFC 6621.

The second rule is new. If the requested TLV type does not immediately define all the corresponding type extensions, then a common name SHOULD NOT be assigned for that TLV type. Instead it is RECOMMENDED that the "description" for the allocated TLV type be "Defined by Type Extension", and that the type extension registry created for the TLV type be named "Type XX Packet TLV Type Extensions", "Type XX Message TLV Type Extensions" or "Type XX Address Block TLV Type Extensions", with XX replaced by the numerical value of the TLV type.

The third recommendation covers how extensions themselves are named. When a new type extension is required, and unless there are reasons to the contrary, the next consecutive type extension is allocated and given a name. The RFC allows reasons to the contrary, which may include maintaining a correspondence between corresponding Packet, Message and Address Block TLVs, and reserving type extension zero if it is not yet allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule for new entries is simple: if a whole family of versions is defined at once, give the family a name. If only one or two versions exist, leave the family unnamed, describe it as defined by its extension, and give each version its own name.

sections.title: The Renamed Registries
sections.content:
Section 3.2 lists every change to the MANET Parameters registry, including corrections of some existing minor errors, and lists unchanged registries for clarity. The "Packet TLV Types" registry is unchanged, as are the "ICV Packet TLV Type Extensions" and "TIMESTAMP Packet TLV Type Extensions" registries.

The "Message TLV Types" registry changes to match Table 1. Types 0 and 1 become "Defined by Type Extension" against RFC 5497, types 2 to 4 are unassigned, type 5 is ICV and type 6 is TIMESTAMP against RFC 7182, types 7 and 8 become "Defined by Type Extension" against RFC 7181, types 9 to 223 are unassigned, and types 224 to 255 are reserved for experimental use. The registries underneath them are renamed to match: "INTERVAL_TIME Message Type Extensions" becomes "Type 0 Message TLV Type Extensions", "VALIDITY_TIME Message Type Extensions" becomes "Type 1 Message TLV Type Extensions", "MPR_WILLING Message Type Extensions" becomes "Type 7 Message TLV Type Extensions", and "CONT_SEQ_NUM Message Type Extensions" becomes "Type 8 Message TLV Type Extensions". The "ICV" and "TIMESTAMP" message registries are unchanged, as are the HELLO, SMF_TYPE and TC message-specific ones.

The "Address Block TLV Types" registry changes to match Table 6. Types 0 and 1 become "Defined by Type Extension" against RFC 5497, types 2, 3 and 4 become "Defined by Type Extension" against RFC 6130, type 5 is ICV and type 6 is TIMESTAMP against RFC 7182, type 7 is LINK_METRIC against RFC 7181, types 8, 9 and 10 become "Defined by Type Extension" against the same RFC, types 11 to 223 are unassigned, and types 224 to 255 are reserved for experimental use. The registries underneath are renamed in the same way: "INTERVAL_TIME", "VALIDITY_TIME", "LOCAL_IF", "LINK_STATUS" and "OTHER_NEIGHB" become the Type 0, Type 1, Type 2, Type 3 and Type 4 Address Block TLV Type Extensions registries, while "MPR", "NBR_ADDR_TYPE" and "GATEWAY" become the Type 8, Type 9 and Type 10 ones. Two registries are renamed without any other change: "ICV Address TLV Type Extensions" becomes "ICV Address Block TLV Type Extensions", and "TIMESTAMP Address TLV Type Extensions" becomes "TIMESTAMP Address Block TLV Type Extensions". The "LINK_METRIC Address Block TLV Type Extensions" registry, which defines all the extensions of its type, is unchanged, as are the HELLO, SMF_NBR_TYPE and TC address block registries. One further change: the document adds reservations for experimental use, following RFC 5226, which RFC 7181 had omitted, to the last three tables.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry entries themselves are rewritten. Most type numbers now say only "Defined by Type Extension", and the lists underneath them are renamed after the number of the type they belong to, such as "Type 3 Address Block TLV Type Extensions".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC has one paragraph here. As the document is concerned only with how entities are named, and those names are used only in documents such as this one and in IANA registries, it has no security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here can affect the security of a network, because the document only changes labels in a registry.

viz.caption: THE TWO WAYS A TLV TYPE IS ALLOCATED

items.title: Type defines all extensions
items.text: A common name is given to the type and to every full type under it. LINK_METRIC is the example.

items.title: Type defines one extension
items.text: The name belongs to the full type only, and the type itself is described as Defined by Type Extension.

items.title: Extension registries
items.text: Each type gets a registry named Type XX ... TLV Type Extensions, with XX the type number.

items.title: No behaviour change
items.text: Only names change. Protocols behave exactly as they did before.
